newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Apr 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Apr 18.

text.p: Threat of legal fight over tribal fish plan: Court action is being threatened by urban Maori authorities after the Waitangi Fisheries Commission announced plans to allocate fisheries assets on the basis of tribes. Page 1.
Winebox inquiry to go ahead as planned: The Winebox inquiry is to continue its programme as planned unless the High Court makes an order preventing it. Page 1.

Estates would get super funds says Peters: All superannuation contributions paid by people who died before retiring would go to the contributor's estate, Treasurer Winston Peters said on Thursday. Page 2.
NZ in air services deal with S Africa: The first bilateral air services treaty between South Africa and New Zealand had been settled, Transport Minister Jenny Shipley said. Page 2.

Audit Office to call for increased powers: The Audit Office wants broader powers to monitor public-sector organisations and says the limitations "frustrated" its review of Te Mangai Paho, the funder of the troubled Aotearoa Television Network. Page 2.

Student Allowance not certain: The coalition agreement committed the government to only look at a universal living allowance for tertiary students within its three-year term, not to introduce one, Education Minister Wyatt Creech said on Thursday. Page 2.
Women MPs unite to fight: A special cross-party caucus of women MPs is being set up to lobby against compulsory superannuation. Page 2.

Funding reduces waiting lists: Health Minister Bill English said a further 7600 people on hospital waiting lists would be offered procedures and treatment after the latest round of allocations from the government's waiting times fund. Page 2.

Nats focus on keeping identity: National's battle to maintain its identity within the government and avoid slipping down the polls with coalition partner NZ First will be a focus of this weekend's half-yearly divisional party conference at Parliament. Page 2.
More banks cut mortgage interest rates: AMP, its niche mortgage provider Ergo, HonkongBank and ASB Bank joined Countrywide Bank in cutting variable mortgage interest rates on Thursday. Page 17.

Revisions take shine of balance of payments figures: Statistical revisions took the shine off better-than-expected balance of payments data issued on Thursday and economists still expect the trend in the data to deteriorate. Page 17.
Brother has full control of winery: One of the two partners in Marlborough's Jackson Estate wine company has sold out to the other. Page 17.

Investors 'attracted by salary disclosures': Revealing all the payments made to executive directors of public companies will make New Zealand companies more attractive to international investors, says American law professor Dale Oesterle. Page 17.

Optomistic ASH pins hopes on Kirton: New Zealand anti-smoking groups are pinning their hopes on Associate Health Minister Neil Kirton to push legal action against tobacco companies, says ASH spokeswoman Trish Fraser. Page 4.

Dole scheme 'foundering': Labour has labelled the government's work for the dole scheme as a "chores for the dole" scheme, after suggestions by Employment Minister Peter McCardle that the unemployed could do household repairs and maintenance. Page 8.

Peters 'will be absorbed into National Party': Former prime minister David Lange says Winston Peters will be absorbed "perfectly nicely and naturally" back into the National Party while New Zealand First becomes a Maori party under the leadership of Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare. Page 8.
Single source for heat, power: The National Library is set to save up to $40,000 a year in energy costs, because of a power generation system developed by Enerco New Zealand. Page 20.
